A great feature that Digg used to have and that reddit doesn't have is allowing users to "catch up" and sort of go "back in time" and find posts that were on the front page previously, so as to not miss a thing.

The way this worked at Digg was as follows:
With Digg, once a submission got popular enough in their new queue, it was allowed on the front page (not page 2, 3 or 4, but the front page), and from then on, it moved down as it got older. This meant that pages 2, 3, 4, etc. were in reverse chronological order, where the further you moved away from the front page, the older posts got, and you could actually click your way through to what was effectively an archive of past front page posts and by the time you got all the way back to posts you had previously seen from the time you last were on the site, you could be sure that you had not have missed anything that had been on the front page since then.

Obviously, this was tied to Digg's ranking mechanism, or in other words, the existence of that feature was a function of Digg's ranking mechanism. Reddit has a different ranking mechanism, which is why this doesn't work on reddit, and if you click from the front page to page 2, 3, 4, etc., while things may be vaguely in reverse chronological order, you do actually have posts in there that are bubbling up, bubbling down, and things are changing all the time, especially with the main front page or in highly active subreddits, so you're almost guaranteed to miss stuff this way.

But it's possible to replicate the desired functionality even without adopting Digg's ranking mechanism: I think voat could and should create a "front page archive", that is a reverse chronological list of submissions that have moved OFF the front page. So every time the front page changes, the submissions no longer on it enter the "wayback front page".

It might be a challenge figuring out how to deal with submissions that move off and then reenter the front page (possibly repeatedly). One solution would be to allow duplicates in the archive (i.e. same submission on page 2 and 4), but eliminate duplicates on the same page of the archive (can't have the same submission twice on page 2).

An archive / time travel / wayback feature like that should allow users to go back through the site and ensure that they didn't miss anything that was on the front page, and things there wouldn't be as haphazard as they often are when browsing reddit.
Suggestion: Allow users to go "back in time" in an archive of past front page posts.

Why is each black box on a plane dedicated to storing only certain information, to the exclusion of other info? Why is there one and only one flight data recorder, and one and only one cockpit voice recorder?

If you're going to install two black boxes (which makes sense), then why not store the flight data and the voice recording in both black boxes? Storage is cheap. Backups are important. If only the contents of one of the black boxes are recoverable, you should still have both the flight and voice data.
Why are the black boxes in planes not mutually redundant?
Good point. I don't know why they aren't mutually redundant either.

The question we should be asking is why do we even have 1950's technology black boxes (well, orange boxes), because that's what they are?

This is in a world where you can pay for high speed wifi internet access so that you can watch cat videos, on the same flight as a CVR that needs to be dredged from the bottom of the ocean or a FDR that's lost in the mountains.

In other words, the industry considers critical and possibly life saving flight parameters and flight tracking to be far less important than wifi for their passengers. Think about that for a moment.

That's a good point. Of course, you have to start somewhere, and eliminating black boxes and replacing them with overconfident reliance in "the cloud" (heh) wouldn't be the right answer either. We should probably have redundant black boxes and encrypted safety data transmission. There's an issue though: Currently, it's my understanding that the black boxes only store so and so much info, and then the old stuff gets overwritten – and this info only gets looked at if there's an actual incident. If all that stuff got transmitted to some server farm somewhere, you could hang on to everything, indefinitely, and corporate and the authorities might be tempted to do that. There might even be a temptation to have the ability to monitor both the flight and voice data live, in real time. That would have some problematic privacy implications. Would you like it if your every move got recorded, permanently, and if you had your boss looking over your shoulder and listen to every word you say for your entire professional life? There's a slippery slope there too, and I wouldn't want to slide down too far.

As for Wifi, actually, speaking as someone who avoids unknown Wifi hotspots run by the Gods know who doing who knows what, I have to show my ignorance and ask: Is there generally an extra fee for inflight Wifi? Even if there isn't, so long as a disaster hasn't already happened, Wifi or no Wifi is probably more of a consumer-visible feature and sales point than whatever the black boxes are doing behind there scenes, so there's pressure to adopt. And generally, IRL security-relevant technologies are slow to change, with a lot of emphasis on tried and tested. Whether that's always a good thing in a rapidly changing technological world is another question.
What money can be made from improving our understanding of how the accidents come about?

In order to prevent moderator abuse of a subverse I suggest each subverse have a ticker showing deleted and hidden posts as, like a subverses private /r/undelete. The ticker would show what moderator was responsible for the content's removal. In the ticker members of the subverse should have the ability to vote that they want the content in the subverse, therefore overruling the subverse moderator. The moderator would not have any access or say over whether the post and its comments are shown in the deleted content ticker.

If it is illegal content or somehow worse then the situation becomes a bit trickier, perhaps the moderators could flag an admin or something.

I would like to see many improvements of transparency, accountability, and checks and balances. Not just with this suggestion but applied across the entire site.
Deleted Content Ticker - Vote to Undelete

I think that more transparency in the actions of moderators and admins will help keep Voat from experiencing similar scenarios to what has been happening with Reddit. The ticker will surely get filled with trolling posts and comments or simply unhelpful/not relative ones, but also there may be instances in which something of value is removed that the majority of the sub users believe should be returned.

I wonder if it would it be possible for each deleted content to be tagged with the name of the moderator (as some subs have multiple) who did the removal? This would enable tracking of specific mod actions to hold individual mods accountable if they are engaging in some shady acts of suppression, for example.

It would definitely be possible to tag the specific moderator who deleted the post and I think the system definitely should.

And it should list the reason the mod gave for removing the post, like spam, or abusive, or rule #6 violation, etc... That way people won't just get angry at the mods and start posting about how their post was removed unfairly. Once Voat grows I can see people sending brigades after the mods if they think they were treated unfairly and just start complaining. If everyone can see the reasoning behind the mod's decision I think it is more likely to start a civil discussion.
